methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective multicenter study comparing 1431 high-volume center (HVC) patients with 971 medium-volume center (MVC) patients; non-randomized design introduces selection bias. Logistic definitions clear: HVCs ≥30 cases/year, MVCs 11-29. Fisher's exact test and ANOVA appropriately used; Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank tests for survival. Multivariate analysis performed to assess center volume as independent factor for PFS. However, baseline imbalances exist (HVC patients younger, fewer comorbidities, higher-risk ESMO-ESGO categories), suggesting selection effects rather than pure center volume effects.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Cohort study demonstrating association between high-volume center treatment and improved PFS/OS in endometrial cancer, addressing practice-relevant question about centralization benefits. However, causal claims limited by observational design and confounding by indication (HVC patients have higher-risk tumors, receiving more aggressive staging/treatment). Provides real-world evidence for guideline recommendations supporting centralized care but not definitive proof of causation.

reporting_quality.justification: Follows STROBE guidelines with clear methods, baseline characteristics, and outcome reporting. Data collection from 2000-2019 across seven Italian hospitals; manual record review conducted. However, lacks pre-registration statement, conflict-of-interest disclosure specifics, and explicit data availability statement. Authors state data will be made available upon request but no repository specified. Missing details on inter-rater reliability for manual abstraction.

novelty_literature.justification: Extends prior literature on centralization benefits in gynecological oncology (established for ovarian cancer) to endometrial cancer, confirming rather than discovering association. Study primarily validates existing guidelines recommending high-volume center management rather than providing novel insights. Definition of 'high-volume' (≥30 cases/year) differs from prior Italian guidelines (≥20), representing incremental refinement rather than novel finding.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized manuscript with clear introduction contextualizing centralization evidence gap in EC. Methods transparent regarding volume definitions and data collection. Results clearly presented with appropriate tables and figures. Discussion thoughtfully compares findings to ovarian cancer literature and discusses potential mechanisms. Limitations section acknowledges selection bias and observational design. Writing is precise and clinically appropriate.

key_strengths: Large multicenter cohort (2402 patients) with comprehensive outcome data including recurrence sites and survival metrics
Addresses practice-relevant question: impact of facility volume on EC treatment and outcomes in real-world setting
Clear demonstration of HVC benefits: lower complication rates, more aggressive staging (higher mean lymph node harvest 21.5 vs 19), improved laparoscopic adoption (58% vs 47%)
Multivariate analysis identifies center volume as independent PFS predictor; stratified outcomes by ESMO-ESGO risk categories strengthen findings
key_concerns: Observational design with selection bias: HVC patients younger, fewer comorbidities, higher-risk ESMO-ESGO categories suggest confounding by indication rather than pure volume effects
Baseline imbalances not fully adjusted in multivariable analysis; patients treated at HVCs appear to have more aggressive disease requiring more intensive management
Lack of propensity score matching or similar technique to balance confounders; claims about causality not fully supported by analytical approach
Study period 2000-2019 spans substantial changes in EC management; temporal trends may confound volume effects
Definition of 'high-volume' (≥30/year) differs from prior Italian guidelines and international standards, limiting comparability
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically sound retrospective cohort study demonstrating real-world benefits of high-volume endometrial cancer centers but limited by observational design and selection bias. Appropriate for Tier 3 journals; minor revisions should better address confounding through propensity score adjustment.
